blocks.text: Here, therefore, the הערבים are nothing other than true ravens, as, after [col. 215] the Greeks, they are understood by Josephus, the Chaldee, the Syriac, Jerome, most of the Hebrews, and all the Doctors of the Church without exception. God says that he commanded them: I have commanded the ravens (he says) to feed thee there. God is indeed said to command even brute animals, as in 2 Paral. VII, 13. If I command the locust to devour the land. Amos IX, 3. And I will command the serpent, and he shall bite them. And Ion. II, 10. (var. 11.) God spoke to the fish, that it should vomit out Jonah upon the land. But in the same way he commands even inanimate things: the heavens, for instance, Es. XLV, 12.; the clouds, Iob. XXXVIII, 11. Psal. LXXVIII, 23. Es. V, 6.; the dawn, Iob. XXXVIII, 12.; the sword, Amos IX, 4. To command brute animals, or clouds, etc., is to use them to carry out his decrees. Kimchi therefore rightly says here: וטעם צויתי ששמתי בלבם להביא לחם ובשר שתי פעמים ביום, I have commanded (the ravens), that is, I have put it into their mind to bring bread and meat twice a day. But it is in a very different way that he says, in the ninth verse of the same chapter, that he commanded the widow to feed Elias. For he had commanded her either by an express word, or by inclining her mind to charity and piety toward the servant of God. It should further be noted that several ravens, not one, were appointed for this task, as ^{a)} Eutychius of Alexandria holds; for one would not have sufficed to carry the food Elias needed. For in the life of Paul the Hermit by Saint Jerome, among [II, 808] certain other things which I confess I do not understand, there is also this: that a single raven brings a whole loaf, enough for the meal of two men, namely Antony and Paul. They look up, he says, and see that a raven had settled on a branch of the tree, which, flying gently down from there, laid a whole loaf before their astonished faces. After it had gone, Well, said Paul, the Lord has sent us a meal, etc. For sixty years now I have always received a piece of half a loaf; but at your coming Christ has doubled the ration for his soldiers. Here, however, the case is different. For it is not one raven bringing food to several, but several bringing it to one. That food was bread and meat. Many of the ancients hold that these were brought separately: bread in the morning and meat in the evening. Athanasius in the Synopsis: Οἱ κόρακες ἔφερον αὐτῷ, διὰ ῥήματα Κυρίου, πρωΐας μὲν ἄρτους, δείλης δὲ κρέα [Hoi korakes epheron autō, dia rhēmata Kyriou, prōïas men artous, deilēs de krea]. Theodoret on 3 Kings, Question 52: Προσέφερον γὰρ οἱ κόρακες ἄρτους μὲν ἕωθεν, δείλης δὲ κρέα [Prosepheron gar hoi korakes artous men heōthen, deilēs de krea]. Augustine, Sermon 146 De tempore: The raven brought the servant of God bread in the morning, meat in the evening. Eutychius, as cited above: وكان غراب ياتيه في كل يوم بالغداة بخبز وبالعشا بلحم ياكله [wa-kāna ghurāb yaʾtīhi fī kull yawm bi-l-ghadāh bi-khubz wa-bi-l-ʿashā bi-laḥm yaʾkuluhu] And it was a raven that brought him every day bread in the morning and meat in the evening, to eat. This is indeed what the Greek version has in most copies; but the Complutensian has more correctly what is found in the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Roman text: ἄρτους καὶ κρέας τὸ πρωῒ, καὶ ἄρτους καὶ κρέας τὸ δείλης [artous kai kreas to prōi, kai artous kai kreas to deilēs]. For God willed that, amid the utmost scarcity of everything, both bread and meat should be brought to his servant, so that the meal might be complete and his providence in preserving him might shine out the more. To the same purpose is the fact that the ravens brought these meals to the Prophet twice a day, morning and evening, namely dinner and supper, at fixed hours. For that both were customary among the Jews is clear from Luc. XIV, 12. And a midday meal is mentioned in Gen. XLIII, 25. Ruth. II, 14. and Act. X, 9. 10.
